claims.statement: EU Regulation 2024/573 provides certification and training requirements for work on stationary refrigeration, air-conditioning and heat-pump equipment involving fluorinated greenhouse gases or relevant alternatives.

The regulation says non-hermetically sealed equipment charged with covered fluorinated gases may be sold to an end user only where evidence shows installation will be performed by a certified undertaking.
Hypothesis: contracted priority slots are scarce enough that OEMs will pay for an independent dispatch layer; neither technician supply nor OEM willingness has been validated.

contrary_evidence: EU rules are phasing down or prohibiting some high-GWP equipment, so the relevant technician and parts mix will change rather than remain permanently scarce in its current form.
Certification establishes a constraint but does not prove that certified capacity is unavailable in the exact target districts or that OEMs will outsource it.

economics.acquisition_route: Map one voivodeship, verify certificates and insurance, reserve 20 weekly slots across five firms, and sell a limited SLA to one installer or importer before expanding territory.
economics.founder_net_worth_path: Unvalidated path: 35 principals plus 1,000 monthly dispatches could produce roughly PLN 7m annual revenue; at 20% operating profit and a 5x value, a 75% founder stake would be about PLN 5.25m. A 7-9 year route depends on multi-region density, signed SLA renewals and no double counting of retained cash.
economics.founder_time: 12-18 hours per week for network setup, triage design and exception management; appoint an operations coordinator once dispatch volume exceeds roughly ten jobs per week.
economics.gross_margin_basis: Unvalidated estimate: 45-65% on administration and software after triage labor and technician-capacity reservation payments; the company avoids owning vans and inventory during validation.
economics.payback: Unvalidated target: 12-20 months at five B2B principals and 80-120 completed dispatches per month.
economics.pricing: Unvalidated hypothesis: PLN 2,000-8,000 monthly per B2B principal plus PLN 350-800 administration per completed dispatch; repair labor, parts and refrigerant are passed through or contracted separately.
economics.retention_or_repeat: Warranty principals renew if completion time, first-visit resolution and claim evidence improve; technicians remain if reserved work raises utilization without payment friction.

fingerprint.compounding_advantage: dense reserved capacity, failure-code history and demonstrated SLA performance improve routing and make the network harder for a new dispatcher to reproduce
fingerprint.customer: heat-pump manufacturers, importers, warranty insurers and installers with geographically fragmented after-sales obligations
fingerprint.distribution_mechanism: sign one regional installer consortium first, then pursue OEM and insurer integrations with measured completion and response data rather than broad consumer advertising
fingerprint.offer_and_business_model: remote fault intake, credential and parts matching, reserved appointment dispatch, evidence capture and SLA reporting sold as managed network software and administration
fingerprint.payer_and_paid_event: the B2B warranty principal pays a monthly network fee and a per-completed-dispatch administration fee; technicians are paid for accepted work under transparent service terms
fingerprint.problem_trigger: cold-weather failure, local backlog, missing technician skill or a warranty response-time breach

founder_fit: Direct operational adjacency to the parents' renewable-installation company.
Automation, routing and failure-data analysis fit the founder's technical strengths.
The pilot can avoid owning vehicles, inventory or a large technician payroll.
B2B channel selling is periodic and measurable rather than dependent on personal media presence.
risks: A dispatch marketplace can fail during peak weather if reserved capacity is not contractually real.
Incorrect remote triage can create safety, warranty and liability exposure.
OEMs may refuse independent warranty authorization or restrict parts and service information.
F-gas and refrigerant transitions can strand technician skills or require retraining.

structure.control_point: contracted priority appointment inventory from certified service firms, organized by territory, refrigerant competence and parts access
structure.critical_dependency: qualified firms must honor reserved slots and OEMs or insurers must authorize and pay the network for covered repairs

thesis: Contract certified refrigeration and heat-pump service firms for reserved weekly repair slots in underserved Polish districts, then sell manufacturers, importers, insurers and larger installers a triaged warranty-dispatch service with measurable response times. The control asset is priority capacity and parts-routing agreements, not an unearned claim of technician exclusivity. Begin as software, call triage and dispatch; only advertise OEM-authorized warranty work where a signed authorization exists.
title: Reserved Heat-Pump Warranty Capacity Network
uncertainties: How many paid warranty jobs are actually delayed by regional capacity rather than parts or approval?
What reservation payment is enough for certified firms to honor priority slots?
Which OEMs permit third-party network administration and evidence submission?
Can remote triage improve first-visit resolution enough to fund the platform fee?
